messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 79
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Vignette:
Priya Sharma is a 79-year-old airline captain who has flown for over four decades, yet she cannot remember the last time she felt safe inside her own home. The house she shares with her husband—a quiet suburban split-level—has become a place of constant scanning. She checks the locks twice before bed, then three times more after she lies down. She wakes at odd hours, convinced she has heard a footstep or a muffled cry, and she lies still, listening, until her heart stops pounding. Her husband sleeps peacefully beside her, but Priya does not trust him to keep watch. She has come to believe that no one can be relied upon, least of all herself.

The source of this vigilance is a memory that does not behave like an ordinary memory. It arrives in disconnected pieces: the smell of burning kerosene from the kitchen stove, the sight of her mother’s sari ripped at the shoulder, a song playing on the radio—a Hindi film melody that now, seven decades later, can still bring the scene rushing back with unbearable vividness. When that song comes on unexpectedly, Priya feels the event is happening right now. The pieces do not fit together into a coherent story; she remembers the sound of a slap, then the sight of a broken bangle on the floor, then her own small hands pressed over her ears. But there is no smooth narrative linking them. The fragments feel more real than anything she has done today—more real than the pre-flight checklist she has completed a thousand times, more real than the coffee she drinks each morning.

Priya grew up in a household where her father’s rages were a weather system she learned to read. He never hit her; he hit her mother, and Priya watched from behind the curtain. She was seven, then eight, then nine. She told herself she would become strong enough to stop it someday. But that day never came. Now, at seventy-nine, she still replays those scenes in her head, and she imagines what she would do if she could go back. In her mind, she has devised elaborate revenge fantasies: she sees herself confronting her father, or someone like him, and she imagines the look of terror on his face before she acts. These fantasies are the only moments when she feels powerful—yet they leave her more unsettled, more convinced that she is a lousy coper who cannot handle even the slightest upset.

Her career has been her refuge. In the cockpit, at 35,000 feet, Priya is in control. But even there, the past intrudes. On layovers, she refuses to sleep in the hotel bed until the early hours of the morning. She stays up watching television, eating whatever is in the minibar, telling herself that if she stays awake she can monitor the room. She has gained weight over the years, a fact she attributes to the eating that helps her manage the restlessness. The hospital smell that sometimes wafts from a first-aid kit on the flight deck can trigger a wave of nausea—she once fainted in a crew lounge after a colleague opened an antiseptic wipe. She cannot explain why that smell is so potent, only that it belongs to the same fragmented world as the song and the burning kerosene.

At home, Priya’s husband has learned to give her space. They do not discuss her childhood. She does not acknowledge that she is irritable, but she knows she snaps at him for leaving a cupboard door open or for humming a tune he cannot help humming. She has become someone who pushes people away, even as she fears being left alone. Sleeping alone—when her husband travels, or when she checks into a hotel—is intolerable, because in an unfamiliar place the fragmented memories crowd in more densely. She delays sleep until exhaustion forces her into bed, and even then she wakes repeatedly to check the door.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was a moment in the cockpit last month. During a pre-flight walk-around, the smell of jet fuel mixed with something else—a faint antiseptic from the lavatory service cart—and she felt the ground tilt. She thought she was going to relive the event in front of her co-pilot. She froze, and for a few seconds she could not remember how to read the instrument panel. No one noticed, but she knew then that she could no longer rely on herself to do the one thing she has always done well. She is afraid that if she does not get help, she will lose her wings. She is more afraid that even if she gets help, she will still be the little girl behind the curtain, unable to stop anything.
